doc.title: Steve Turré interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 29, 2021

chapter: Rahsaan Roland Kirk and the conch shell
title: Vic Dickinson, 'In a Sentimental Mood', and going back to move forward
summary: Rahsaan plays him Vic Dickinson and Trummy Young records; Turré can't match the deliberate slide, learning that how far back you go decides how far forward.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: Yeah. And he could fix them. He knew how to fix them and stuff. Rubber bands if the springs weren’t right he’d put rubber bands on them and all kinds of stuff you know. And masking tape. He had all kinds of stuff he’d do but he made it work. So you know, so he took me up to his hotel room. And he put on some records like Vic Dickinson and Trummy Young and people in between New Orleans and Lawrence Brown, people in between J.J. and New Orleans. And then I said, “Oh yeah, I like that, I like that. “But J.J.” he said, “J.J. nothing. You try to play this. Get the record and try to play this.” I went and got the record and tried to play what Vic Dickinson was playing on “In a Sentimental Mood” and I couldn’t do it. Because he was using the slide but it wasn’t slop. A lot of trombone players slide around the notes. But I can tell by listening and then knowing the history of the music that it’s slop. That they’re doing it because they can’t really do it clean so they make that part of the thing. But when Vic Dickinson does it it’s deliberate and it’s expressive and it’s accurate and in tune and it makes total music sense. And there’s this recording of Vic Dickinson playing “In a Sentimental Mood” on a Sidney Bechet record. It’s a live recording. Amazing. And that really woke me up and I realized what Rahsaan told me. He said, “As far back as you can go will directly determine how far forward you can go.” If you don’t have a good root the tree doesn’t grow strong and bear fruit.
